title: A combinatorial framework for clustering graph states: Algorithms and hardness for rank-integrity
authors: Romain Bourneuf, Nathan Claudet, Sang Yoon Kim, Rose McCarty, Blair D. Sullivan, Stéphan Thomassé
abstract: We introduce a new notion of distance between two graph states $|G\rangle$ and $|G'\rangle$ on the same set of qubits. This distance is the minimum number of ancilla qubits in a graph state $|\widehat{G}\rangle$ from which both $|G\rangle$ and $|G'\rangle$ can be ``easily prepared''. (When preparing graph states, we are only allowed to use one-qubit Clifford gates, one-qubit Pauli measurements, and classical communication.) We give a graphical description of this distance through the lens of vertex-minors. We then show how this distance yields quantum network analogs of many graph edit-distance problems.   Using this framework, we develop classical algorithms for identifying the ``highly entangled clusters'' of a graph state $|G\rangle$. The ancilla integrity problem asks, given a graph $G$ and integer $k$, for the minimum -- over all graph states $|G'\rangle$ with distance at most $k$ from $|G\rangle$ -- of the maximum component size of $G'$. Up to a factor of $2$ in the number of ancilla qubits, this problem is equivalent to rank integrity, where the distance between $G$ and $G'$ is instead the minimum rank of the sum of their adjacency matrices over $\text{GF}(2)$. We prove that rank integrity is XP parameterized by $k$. We also prove the complementary hardness result that rank integrity is W[1]-hard in $k$. Finally, we give an explicit $\mathcal{O}(n^6)$-time algorithm for ancilla integrity when $G$ has $n$ vertices and $k=1$.
summary: This paper introduces a combinatorial framework to measure the 'distance' between quantum graph states. This distance metric is shown to be equivalent to a graph property called rank integrity, which measures how much two graphs can differ while keeping the rank of their combined adjacency matrix low. The work provides both efficient algorithms and hardness results for determining this structural parameter.
main_problem: The paper develops a combinatorial framework to analyze clustering graph states, which is mathematically related to quantum network edit-distance problems.
main_result: It establishes that the ancilla integrity problem for graph states is equivalent to rank integrity, proving this latter problem is XP parameterized by $k$ but also W[1]-hard in $k$.
method: The authors use concepts from graph theory (vertex-minors, local complementation) and algebraic methods over GF(2) to translate quantum state distance into computable graph properties.
model_or_system: The primary model is the graph state $|	ext{G}angle$ on qubits, which represents a quantum network resource. The analysis focuses on how these states can be related or perturbed using limited quantum operations (Clifford gates and Pauli measurements).
key_observables: The minimum number of ancilla qubits required to prepare two graph states, the maximum component size of the resulting cluster state $G'$, and the rank of the sum of adjacency matrices over GF(2).
important_parameters: The parameter $k$, which quantifies the allowed 'distance' or perturbation level between graph states.
main_assumptions: The distance measure is restricted to preparation using one-qubit Clifford gates, Pauli measurements, and classical communication.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates a graph $G'$ obtained from $G$ by flipping, and the resulting sum graph $G + G'$, connecting structural changes to rank properties.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the distance metric, relates it combinatorially to vertex-minors, establishes equivalence with rank integrity, and then proves complexity results (XP vs. W[1]-hardness) for solving this parameterized problem.
why_interesting: It provides a deep mathematical link between graph structure theory (edit distances) and the resource quantification of quantum entanglement in network models, which is crucial for understanding computational limits in measurement-based quantum computation.
